questions.stem: The modern system of sovereign nation-states is usually traced to the:
options: Treaty of Versailles of 1919
Signing of the UN Charter in 1945
Magna Carta signed in 1215
Peace of Westphalia of 1648
questions.explanation: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War and is credited with establishing the principle that each state has supreme authority over its own territory. The UN Charter came much later and built on that principle.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the need for international relations in the global community?
options: International relations matter only in wartime, because states have no reason to cooperate during peace
Problems such as climate change, pandemics and conflict cross borders and cannot be solved by one state alone
International relations allow larger states to make laws that apply directly inside every smaller state they deal with
International relations replace domestic law, so states no longer need their own parliaments or courts
questions.explanation: Global issues require cooperation through treaties, organisations and diplomacy because their causes and effects cross borders. International law does not replace domestic law, and no state can legislate for another.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how state sovereignty limits the protection of human rights?
options: Sovereignty applies only to small states, so powerful states are always subject to the jurisdiction of international courts
Sovereignty means that every human rights treaty is binding on every state, whether or not that state has agreed to it
A state can refuse to ratify a treaty or accept a court's jurisdiction, and there is no global police force to compel it
A state that ratifies a treaty automatically loses control of its own laws to the United Nations General Assembly
questions.explanation: International law largely depends on state consent, so a state may stay outside a treaty or ignore a ruling with limited consequences. Ratifying a treaty creates obligations, but it does not hand control of domestic law to the UN.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an international organisation fostering relationships in the global community?
options: A state court sentencing an offender for an assault in a suburban street
A local council approving the construction of a new playground in a park
The World Health Organization coordinating states' responses to a pandemic
A national parliament passing a law on the speed limit on its own highways
questions.explanation: International organisations such as the WHO bring states together to share information and coordinate action on shared problems. The other examples are purely domestic decisions by a single state's institutions.

questions.stem: Human rights are described as universal. This means they:
options: belong only to citizens who have reached the age of majority
may be removed by a government when it judges this to be necessary
belong to every person everywhere, simply because they are human
apply only in countries that have passed a bill of rights into law
questions.explanation: Universality means human rights belong to all people regardless of nationality, sex, race or any other status. They are also described as inalienable, meaning they cannot be given up or taken away, although some may be lawfully limited.

questions.stem: Human rights are described as indivisible and interdependent. Which example best shows this?
options: Without an adequate education, a person may be unable to take part effectively in political life
A state may choose to protect civil rights fully while treating economic rights as entirely optional
A person who breaks the law permanently loses all their human rights in every area of life
Each right exists on its own, so a breach of one right never affects any other right
questions.explanation: Indivisibility means rights depend on one another, so denying one, such as education, undermines others, such as political participation. Rights are not optional extras, and people do not lose all rights by breaking the law.

questions.stem: Civil and political rights, such as freedom of speech and the right to a fair trial, are often called:
options: second-generation rights
third-generation rights
collective rights
first-generation rights
questions.explanation: Civil and political rights developed first and protect individuals from abuse of state power. Economic, social and cultural rights are second-generation rights, and collective rights such as self-determination and environmental rights are third-generation rights.

questions.stem: Which right is an example of an economic, social and cultural right?
options: The right to an adequate standard of living, including food and housing
The right to vote in genuine periodic elections held by a secret ballot
The right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion
The right not to be subjected to arbitrary arrest or detention
questions.explanation: The right to an adequate standard of living is protected by the ICESCR and requires positive action by states. Voting, freedom of religion and freedom from arbitrary detention are civil and political rights in the ICCPR.

questions.stem: The right of peoples to self-determination is set out in Article 1 of:
options: the UN Charter only, and no treaty
the Rome Statute of the ICC
the Convention on the Rights of the Child
both the ICCPR and the ICESCR
questions.explanation: Common Article 1 of both covenants states that all peoples have the right of self-determination, allowing them to determine their political status and pursue their economic, social and cultural development. It is a collective right held by peoples rather than individuals.

questions.stem: In 2022 the UN General Assembly recognised the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. What does this best show about human rights?
options: Environmental rights are now enforceable in every domestic court in the world
The General Assembly can create treaties that bind states without their consent
Third-generation rights have replaced civil and political rights in importance
Recognition of rights changes over time as new threats to human dignity emerge
questions.explanation: The resolution reflects the developing recognition of rights in response to issues such as climate change. General Assembly resolutions are not binding treaties, so recognition does not by itself make the right enforceable.

questions.stem: The International Bill of Human Rights consists of the:
options: ICCPR, the ICESCR and the UN Charter
UDHR, the ICCPR and the ICESCR
UN Charter, the UDHR and the Rome Statute
UDHR, the Geneva Conventions and the CRC
questions.explanation: The International Bill of Human Rights is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the two covenants of 1966, together with the optional protocols to the ICCPR. The Geneva Conventions concern conduct in armed conflict, and the Rome Statute set up the ICC.

questions.stem: The ICCPR and ICESCR were adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1966. Why did they take until 1976 to come into force?
options: Each needed to be ratified by a minimum number of states before it became binding
Each had to be approved by a unanimous vote of the Security Council before taking effect
Each had to be translated into every language spoken in every member state first
Each needed the International Court of Justice to rule on whether it was lawful
questions.explanation: Multilateral treaties usually specify that they enter into force once a set number of states, 35 in the case of the covenants, have ratified them. The Security Council and the ICJ have no role in bringing a treaty into force.

questions.stem: Which statement about the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) is correct?
options: It is a non-binding declaration that Australia voted against in 2007 and endorsed in 2009
It is a binding treaty that Australia ratified in 2007, making its rights enforceable in court
It was drafted by the Australian Parliament and later adopted by the UN General Assembly
It applies only to Indigenous peoples in states that have not yet become UN member states
questions.explanation: UNDRIP was adopted by the General Assembly in 2007 with four states, including Australia, voting against; Australia formally endorsed it in 2009. As a declaration it sets standards but is not legally binding unless its principles are incorporated into domestic law.

questions.stem: What is the Universal Periodic Review of the UN Human Rights Council?
options: A vote of the Security Council every year on which states should face military action
A process in which the human rights record of every UN member state is reviewed by other states
A court that tries individuals accused of genocide and crimes against humanity anywhere in the world
A tribunal that hears complaints only against states that have not ratified the ICCPR
questions.explanation: Under the UPR, every member state's human rights record is examined in turn and other states make recommendations. It relies on peer pressure rather than enforcement, which is a strength for universality and a weakness for compliance.

questions.stem: The UN Human Rights Council was created in 2006 to replace the:
options: Trusteeship Council
League of Nations
Commission on Human Rights
International Court of Justice
questions.explanation: The Human Rights Council replaced the Commission on Human Rights, which had been criticised for allowing states with poor records to shield one another. The Trusteeship Council is a separate UN organ that suspended operation in 1994.

questions.stem: How do UN treaty bodies, such as the Human Rights Committee, monitor states' compliance with human rights treaties?
options: By imposing fines on states that the Security Council must then collect from them
By removing states from the United Nations if their reports are submitted late
By examining periodic reports that states must submit and issuing concluding observations
By sending peacekeeping forces to any state that the committee finds has breached the treaty
questions.explanation: States parties report regularly, and the treaty body reviews the report, often alongside NGO shadow reports, before making recommendations. The committees have no power to fine states, deploy forces or expel members.

questions.stem: Australia has accepted the First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR. What does this allow?
options: The Human Rights Committee to strike down any Australian law that it finds breaches the covenant
The International Criminal Court to try Australian politicians for breaches of civil rights
Australian courts to enforce the ICCPR directly without any legislation being passed by Parliament
Individuals in Australia to complain to the Human Rights Committee after exhausting domestic remedies
questions.explanation: The First Optional Protocol allows individual communications, as in Toonen v Australia (1994). The Committee's views are not binding and it cannot strike down laws, so their effect depends on the state's response.

questions.stem: Which is a main limitation of the UN in protecting human rights?
options: The UN has no power to set standards because no human rights treaties have ever been adopted
The UN can only act inside states that have first been invited to join the Security Council as members
The UN is required to use military force against any state found to have breached a treaty
Any of the five permanent members can veto Security Council action, even in a human rights crisis
questions.explanation: The veto means geopolitical interests can block action to stop serious abuses. The UN has adopted many human rights treaties, and it is not obliged to use force against states that breach them.

questions.stem: Which statement about the International Criminal Court is correct?
options: It tries states, not individuals, and can order them to pay compensation to victims
It tries individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression
It hears disputes between states about borders and the interpretation of treaties
It hears appeals from the highest courts of every member country on human rights questions
questions.explanation: The ICC, set up by the Rome Statute and operating since 2002, prosecutes individuals for the most serious international crimes. Disputes between states go to the International Court of Justice.

questions.stem: The ICC acts on the principle of complementarity. This means it:
options: replaces national courts entirely for any offence that involves a breach of human rights
acts only when national courts are unwilling or genuinely unable to investigate or prosecute
acts only after the UN General Assembly votes unanimously to refer each situation to the court
shares each trial equally with a court of the accused's own country, with joint judges
questions.explanation: Complementarity leaves national courts with primary responsibility, so the ICC steps in only where states fail to act genuinely. This respects sovereignty but means many crimes depend on domestic action.

questions.stem: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (1993) and for Rwanda (1994) were established by the:
options: Human Rights Council
UN Security Council
UN General Assembly
International Court of Justice
questions.explanation: The Security Council created these ad hoc tribunals under its Chapter VII powers to prosecute individuals for atrocities in those conflicts. Their experience helped shape the permanent International Criminal Court.

questions.stem: Australia has ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child. How do its protections become part of Australian domestic law?
options: Each state must hold a referendum to approve the convention for its residents
Parliament must pass legislation giving effect to the convention's obligations
The convention becomes domestic law automatically on the date it is ratified
The High Court must declare the convention valid in a special hearing
questions.explanation: Australia follows a dualist approach: a ratified treaty creates international obligations but is not part of domestic law until Parliament legislates. Ratification can still influence how courts interpret ambiguous laws.

questions.stem: The Australian Human Rights Commission is established under the:
options: Racial Discrimination Act 1975
Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986
Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011
questions.explanation: The Commission was created in 1986 as the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission and later renamed; its Act is now called the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986. The Racial Discrimination Act is one of the federal discrimination laws it administers.

questions.stem: Which is a function of the Australian Human Rights Commission?
options: Investigating and conciliating complaints of discrimination under federal law
Striking down Commonwealth laws that are inconsistent with human rights treaties
Prosecuting people who commit crimes against humanity in Australian courts
Hearing appeals from the High Court on questions of human rights law
questions.explanation: The AHRC investigates and conciliates complaints, educates the public, conducts inquiries and advises Parliament. It cannot invalidate laws or make binding decisions, which limits its power.

questions.stem: A complaint of unlawful discrimination to the Australian Human Rights Commission cannot be resolved by conciliation and is terminated. What can the complainant then do?
options: Apply to the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court for a binding decision
Ask the Commission itself to make a binding order that the respondent must pay compensation
Appeal to the UN Human Rights Council, which can order the respondent to pay damages
Ask the Commonwealth Ombudsman to rehear the complaint and impose a penalty
questions.explanation: If conciliation fails, the complainant may take the matter to the federal courts, which can make enforceable orders such as damages. The Commission itself cannot make binding determinations.

questions.stem: Under the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011, a member introducing a bill into the Commonwealth Parliament must:
options: obtain a ruling from the High Court that the bill does not breach any international treaty
hold a referendum if the bill limits any right protected in an international treaty
table a statement of compatibility assessing the bill against seven core human rights treaties
obtain the written approval of the Australian Human Rights Commission before the bill can be debated
questions.explanation: Statements of compatibility and the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights encourage Parliament to consider rights. Parliament can still pass a bill that is incompatible, so the protection is procedural rather than binding.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the protection of human rights through statute law in Australia?
options: Statutes can be made only by the High Court, so they lack democratic legitimacy as a source of rights
Statutes can protect rights in detail and be updated easily, but Parliament can also amend or repeal them
Statutes cannot be changed once passed, so they give stronger protection than the Constitution provides
Statutes protect every right listed in the ICCPR and ICESCR, so no further protection is needed
questions.explanation: Laws such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 provide detailed, enforceable protection, but they lack the entrenchment of constitutional rights. Parliament has at times suspended statutory protections, showing their vulnerability.

questions.stem: Which Australian jurisdictions currently have a human rights Act or charter?
options: Only the Commonwealth Parliament
Every state and territory in Australia
The ACT, Victoria and Queensland
New South Wales and Western Australia
questions.explanation: The ACT (2004), Victoria (2006) and Queensland (2019) have enacted human rights legislation. NSW and the Commonwealth have no general human rights Act, which is central to debates over a national framework.

questions.stem: Which argument is commonly made against a federal Human Rights Act?
options: It would make every international treaty part of Australian law without any further legislation
It would abolish the existing federal anti-discrimination Acts and the Human Rights Commission
It would require a referendum to change any law, so Parliament could no longer legislate
It could shift decisions on contested social questions from elected parliaments to unelected judges
questions.explanation: Opponents argue that existing parliamentary democracy and the common law protect rights well, and that judges should not decide value-laden issues. Supporters argue Australia is the only liberal democracy without a national bill of rights and that current protection is patchy.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument for a federal Human Rights Act in Australia?
options: A federal Act would allow the High Court to remove members of Parliament who breach human rights
Rights protection is currently fragmented, with few express constitutional rights and no national charter
The Constitution already protects all the rights in the ICCPR, so a new Act would add consistency
A federal Act would stop states and territories from passing any human rights laws of their own
questions.explanation: Supporters point to the limited express rights in the Constitution and the patchwork of statutes and common law, arguing a single Act would improve protection and accountability. The Constitution protects only a handful of rights, not those of the ICCPR.

questions.stem: Which is an example of promoting human rights through education?
options: An organisation running school programs so young people understand their rights
A court sentencing a person for an assault committed in a public place
A government banning a newspaper from reporting on a particular human rights abuse
A state refusing to submit its periodic report to a UN treaty body
questions.explanation: Education builds awareness of rights so people can recognise and challenge breaches. Sentencing an offender is enforcement of criminal law, and banning reporting or refusing to report undermines promotion.

questions.stem: An NGO publishes a detailed report documenting abuses in a country's prisons, based on interviews with former detainees. Which method of promotion does this mainly show?
options: Litigation
Investigation
Persuasion
Education
questions.explanation: Investigating and documenting abuses produces evidence that can be used to pressure governments and inform UN bodies. Persuasion and advocacy then use that evidence to push for change.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the role of NGOs such as Amnesty International in promoting human rights?
options: They are funded and directed by governments, so they cannot criticise any state's human rights record
They can only act in states that have no domestic human rights laws, which limits them to a few countries
They raise awareness and pressure governments, but they cannot make binding decisions or enforce compliance
They make binding rulings on human rights breaches that every UN member state must accept and enforce
questions.explanation: NGOs investigate, campaign, lobby and submit shadow reports, and their independence gives them credibility. They have no legal power to enforce their findings, so their effect depends on public and political pressure.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Coalition of Peaks is correct?
options: It is a committee of the NSW Parliament that reviews bills for their effect on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
It is a group of community-controlled peak organisations that are parties to the 2020 National Agreement on Closing the Gap
It is a UN body that hears individual complaints from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people about breaches of the ICCPR
It is a federal court created to hear native title claims and decide disputes between land councils and governments
questions.explanation: The Coalition of Peaks brings together community-controlled peak organisations and is a party, with all Australian governments, to the National Agreement on Closing the Gap. Its role reflects the principle that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people should share in decisions affecting them.

questions.stem: Which is a main strength of the media in promoting human rights?
options: The media can prosecute officials for abuses that their own governments have failed to address
Reporting can expose abuses quickly to a wide audience and pressure governments to respond
Media outlets can order governments to stop abuses through binding legal judgments
The media always reports every human rights issue in a balanced and complete way
questions.explanation: Coverage, including social media, can bring hidden abuses to public attention and create pressure for change. The media has no legal power to make binding orders or prosecute.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation of the media in promoting human rights?
options: The media can report only on human rights issues that take place inside its own country
Coverage is selective and short-lived, and in some states the media is censored or controlled
The media is prohibited by international law from reporting on any breach of human rights
Reporting on human rights abuses can occur only after a UN court has delivered a judgment
questions.explanation: Media attention moves on quickly, focuses on dramatic stories and can be biased, while authoritarian states restrict reporting. These factors mean many abuses receive little sustained attention.

questions.stem: Which method of promoting human rights involves directly lobbying governments and decision-makers to change laws or policies?
options: Education
Investigation
Adjudication
Advocacy
questions.explanation: Advocacy involves speaking up for a cause, campaigning and lobbying decision-makers for change. Investigation gathers evidence, and adjudication is decision-making by a court or tribunal.
